body:
The [concerns](https://github.com/w3c-fedid/digital-credentials/blob/main/custom-schemes.md) of using custom schemes for digital credentials are well documented, so it seems inappropriate to add this as a custom scheme. 

The [Digital Credentials](https://www.w3.org/TR/digital-credentials/) spec provides a more secure and privacy preserving solution to what the `openid4vp:` scheme. Further, browser vendors are working together to support the Digital Credentials API precisely so custom schemes are not needed. To quote the W3C spec:

> As documented in [Presenting Credentials on the Web](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Ppaz_EnhzHqPOz5UusRJvbSunh-RXPWgJ3Np_TM2EE0/) and [Concerns with custom schemes for identity presentment](https://github.com/w3c-fedid/digital-credentials/blob/main/custom-schemes.md), those solutions have security, privacy, and accessibility concerns.

The [Digital Credentials](https://www.w3.org/TR/digital-credentials/) specification does not currently define a solution for web wallets and I don't see how it could serve as an alternative for the time being 

At present, both the spec and its technical previews are scoped solely to native applications integrated through the OS. No mechanism is provided for PWAs or similar to register as wallets. As a result, in-browser invocation of a wallet via the `openid4vp:` protocol is not currently feasible.

By contrast, safelisting the `openid4vp:` protocol provides a functional option, and it is preferable to have an option, even with certain [navigation limitations](https://github.com/w3c-fedid/digital-credentials/blob/main/custom-schemes.md#user-experience-concerns),  rather than no option and a hardcoded native-app-only path. Of course, a DC API approach that also worked for web wallets would be an even better solution.


Two complementary notes:

* The `openid4vp:` scheme is not an arbitrary, application-specific custom URI and should not be treated as such. It is registered with IANA and defined by a formal specification (more formal than the supporting documents of other safelisted schemes) enabling standardized interaction across deployed wallets and verifiers

* The wallet is one component of a three-pillar model, alongside the issuer and the verifier. The game changer here is the trust layer that binds these pillars, which is often overlooked in the context of the DC API. The due-diligence processes required by each trust model (e.g., EUDI or domain-specific) during a presentation request would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to implement at the OS level without reintroducing the friction and redundancy that the original designs sought to avoid. Also the argument of minimum security safeguards is insufficient: in most cases, the current matching and selection proposal at the credential level would either be redundant due to the already strict in-wallet presentation policies (disclosure, entitlement policies) enforced by domain-specific rulebooks, or unnecessarily complex for simple use cases such as loyalty card sharing

Right, but the protocol is OpenID application specific. The API is protocol agnostic. If this protocol was actually to serve “web wallets” it would be protocol agnostic too (I.e., wallet: or whatever, similar to mailto:, which doesn’t tie itself to a particular format). 

Also, just defining the protocol doesn’t provide the security assurances the API does: one can still craft any URL with openid4vp:, while the DC API encourages data sanitation through IDL conversion.

Given the high value of these credentials, there are safer alternative means that web applications could use to identify themselves as “web wallets” than by using protocol schemes.

Please also take a look at @martinthomson's comments about this: 
https://github.com/mozilla/standards-positions/issues/1003#issuecomment-3212917334

@marcoscaceres  Exactly my point. 

`openid4vp:` is protocol-specific and comes with legitimacy checks and trust frameworks governed by domain owners: trustworthy issuers provide credentials to trustworthy wallets. In this model, trustworthiness is a chain effect, established well before wallet invocation. We cannot take this out of the equation. That's why `openid4vp:` should remain an option

On the other hand, the DC API is indeed protocol-agnostic and therefore must define a bare-minimum trust model, which seems to be anchored on wallets pre-registered with the operating system (i.e., OS bindings are required)

Consequently, this raises the question: is the DC API a spec designed for wallets distributed via mobile OS app stores and effectively tied to the OS vendor ecosystem for trust? If that is the case, then this would be my second argument for safelisting `openid4vp:` to safeguard diversity and domain-based trust control

Regarding mozilla’s team response you referenced: 

as everything is still at a very early stage, I don’t agree with the premature adoption of a paternalistic stance on the basis of hypothetical inefficiencies or risks in wallet flows. On the contrary, it is just as likely that OS platforms will introduce unnecessary burdens and confusion, especially given the existence of high-trust frameworks such as EUDI

My understanding of the principle behind the safelist here is that we're worried about applications which were not designed with the hostility of the open web in mind. I talked briefly to Nikos about this scenario and was originally thinking that of course `openid4vp://` is designed for web hostility and so had no good reason to be excluded from this safelist, and so encouraged him to file this issue. I am very sympathetic to the argument that we've punted on the wallets as PWAs scenario with the Digital Credentials API, so as long as the DC API doesn't support the use case, I find I cannot really complain about such web wallets having to rely on custom schemes.

However, thinking more deeply about this now, the attack vector that matters is that of a malicious web application attempting to attack well-meaning RPs by tricking users to accept registration for `openid4vp://`. Regularly in our Digital Credentials threat-modelling we find ourselves falling back on "users have to trust the wallets they've chosen to install, and actively malicious or irreparably insecure wallets will be kicked out of their app stores". We do not have a threat model for malicious wallets on the open web. Even though such a malicious web application should never be able to get real high-value credentials issued to it, it could still learn what website the user was on when attempting to use a digital credential (for example, when attempting to verify their age on an adult content site). This seems like a non-trivial risk to me that would require at least some real threat-modelling and mitigations. 

In addition there is significant concern around the privacy and security of systems like EUDI, and so any real additional risk poses a risk to the reputation of the whole system. So I think then that I agree with Marcos, for Chromium we're unlikely to be able to add this to our scheme safelist. Also note that (at least for scenarios supported by the DC API), Chrome will [likely](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/440387001) soon start displaying a warning on invocation of custom schemes.
